Counterfactuals in LCA—how can they be made more robust? Counterfactuals in Energy, Economy, & Environment (E3) Models

Date: 09/17/2026
Contact: Matthew Jamieson

In this special session, the working group will share the definitions of the word “counterfactual” and how it may or may not be appropriately used in LCA. In this presentation, the working group will discuss the results of a literature review of how counterfactuals have been used in energy, economy, and environment (E3) models, for example integrated assessment models.

Evaluation of Energy Intensity and EROI of CO2-EOR Pathways: The NETL CELiC Model and Co-product Management

Date: 09/16/2026
Contact: Matthew Jamieson

This presentation for ACLCA 2026 provides a short description of carbon dioxide (CO2)-enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) and tools provided by NETL for analysis of CO2-EOR. The CO2-EOR Life Cycle (CELiC) Model is among those tools and has recently been converted to open LCA to allow for a wider array of industrial CO2 sources and the data to implement various energy analyses, including cumulative energy demand and net energy analysis. Results for CO2 from power plants with post-combustion capture are provided with different co-product management methods and net energy analysis approaches.

A Perspective on Produced Water Realities and Opportunities in Appalachia

Date: 06/18/2026
Contact: Markus Drouven

Produced water management is becoming a strategic issue for Appalachian natural gas development. While national conversations often focus on disposal constraints, desalination, and beneficial reuse, Appalachian produced water realities are markedly different from those in other major U.S. basins. This presentation examines recent produced water production, recycling, sharing, and water-demand trends across Pennsylvania and Northeastern Pennsylvania, highlighting how operators are already relying heavily on recycling and cross-operator water exchanges to sustain development. This discussion explores how produced water management challenges evolve under both high- and low-gas-price scenarios, why water logistics may become an increasingly important operational constraint, and where emerging technologies and decision-support tools can help. The presentation will also introduce AquaTrade—a DOE/NETL-developed, free and open-source produced water exchange platform now adopted in the Permian Basin—and discuss its potential applicability to Appalachian operations. Markus will provide his perspective on how produced water management may influence the future competitiveness, resilience, and growth of natural gas development in the region.

Contact: Markus Drouven
